analysis.one_liner: Pays kidney donors a refundable tax credit of $10,000 a year for five years.
analysis.headline: With 18 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill sat in House committees from August 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give anyone who donates a kidney to a stranger a refundable federal tax credit of $10,000 per year for five years — $50,000 total, paid even to people who owe little or no income tax. If the donor dies during that period, the remaining balance is paid in one lump sum to their estate. The credit applies only to "non-directed" donations, meaning the donor gives to an anonymous stranger rather than to a relative or friend, and it would run for donations made from 2025 through the end of 2034. The bill also amends the 1984 law banning payment for organs to state that this tax credit does not count as illegal payment for a kidney.
analysis.who_benefits: People with kidney failure waiting for a transplant — more than 90,000 Americans are on the national kidney waitlist, and hundreds die each year while waiting. A bigger supply of donated kidneys means shorter waits, fewer years on dialysis, and fewer deaths. Donors themselves also benefit: the credit is refundable and paid over five years, and if a donor dies, their family collects the remainder. Relatives of dialysis patients benefit too, since dialysis is exhausting, costly, and often keeps people out of work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Kidney failure patients on the waitlist

how_it_helps.text: Donors who give a kidney to a stranger would receive a refundable tax credit of $10,000 per year for the donation year and the four following years — $50,000 total, with no requirement to owe income tax to collect it [S2].
If a donor dies during the five-year period, the remaining unpaid balance is accelerated and paid for that tax year, so the family recovers the rest of the $50,000 [S2].

The credit is limited to non-directed donations — giving to an anonymous stranger — so it targets the donor shortage for the national waiting list rather than rewarding people who already planned to donate to a relative [S2].
The bill amends the National Organ Transplant Act's ban on paying for organs to state that this credit is not 'valuable consideration,' clearing the legal way for the payments [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the $50,000-per-donor credits. Because the credit is refundable, the government pays it out even to donors with little or no income tax liability, so the full cost shows up as federal spending. There is a longer-run offset: taxpayers and Medicare pay heavily for dialysis, and each successful transplant eventually replaces years of dialysis care at far lower annual cost — though the savings arrive years after the credits are paid.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts its tax credit from the 1984 National Organ Transplant Act ban on giving 'valuable consideration' for organs. Opponents of paying donors argue that $50,000 could pressure financially desperate people — disproportionately lower-income Americans — into major surgery they would otherwise decline [S2].

The credit costs $50,000 per donor and is refundable, so it is a direct federal outlay even for donors who owe no tax; the bill text sets no cap on total donations and no income limit on who can claim it [S2].

Money alone does not remove the main barriers for many potential donors — lost wages during recovery, job risks, and medical screening costs are not addressed by this bill, so the credit may draw fewer donors than its headline number suggests (bill text contains no wage-protection or cost-reimbursement provisions) [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The humanitarian upside is large: kidney failure is fatal without dialysis or transplant, dialysis is grueling and enormously expensive for Medicare, and the waitlist grows every year because too few living people donate. Against that, the bill's design raises a real ethical objection — it is the first federal step toward paying people for an organ, with a carve-out written into the very law that bans the practice — and $50,000 per donor with no overall cap is an open-ended federal commitment. A well-designed version might pair payments with stronger donor protections and a cost cap; this bill did neither. The core idea addresses a genuine shortage with a genuine shortage with a genuine tool, but the safeguards are thin.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in August 2024 and sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, then routed to a Health subcommittee in December; neither committee ever voted on it, and the Congress ended with the bill still in committee.

narrative.text: Representative Nicole Malliotakis introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, near the end of the two-year Congress, joined by Representatives Harder, Bacon, and Neguse [S2].
It was referred to two committees — Ways and Means (which handles tax credits) and Energy and Commerce (which handles organ transplant policy) — meaning it needed attention from both to move [S4].
Eighteen members signed on as cosponsors, split 13 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S3].
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — a further step down, not a step toward a floor vote [S4].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and all activity ended when the 118th Congress expired on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained directly from the bill dying — the kidney shortage it targeted is unchanged. But the status quo held: dialysis providers keep the patients who would otherwise move to transplants, and the legal wall against paying organ donors stayed intact, which satisfies those who opposed compensated donation on principle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: dialysis providers, and the waitlist keeps growing

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — 18 cosponsors split 13 Democrats and 5 Republicans — and the original four sponsors included two Republicans and two Democrats; the bill died in committee, not on the floor [S3].

industries.industry: Dialysis providers (dialysis clinics and their corporate owners)
industries.note: Dialysis is a multi-billion-dollar industry whose revenue depends on patients remaining on dialysis; a larger supply of living-donor kidneys moves more patients off dialysis and onto transplants, which are cheaper and better for patients. The bill's failure preserves the existing dialysis patient base. No dialysis company's position appears in the congressional record; this is the industry's structural stake in the outcome.

More living-donor kidneys means more transplant surgeries, which transplant centers are paid to perform. The industry's gain here runs alongside the patient's gain — patients on the waitlist need exactly these surgeries.

industries.industry: Organ procurement and transplant coordination organizations
industries.note: An expanded living-donor pipeline would increase matching, evaluation, and coordination work these organizations perform, while also adding donor-safety screening duties. Their core mission — more transplants — aligns with patients' interests.
